notes.meaning: God deliberately allowed several enemy nations to stay in Canaan. The younger generations of Israelites had not lived through Joshua's conquest battles. God used these surrounding nations to test Israel's trust and commitment to Him.

God also left these enemies so that future generations would learn how to fight in battle. Without hardships, living in a rich and easy land could have made the people careless and weak. Most importantly, facing conflict would teach them that true victory comes only from relying on the Lord.

The remaining groups included the five Philistine rulers, all the Canaanites, the Sidonians, and the Hivites in the northern mountains of Lebanon. These groups occupied key positions on the western coast and along the northern border. Because Joshua had not conquered these outer regions, they stayed behind as constant threats.

These nations remained in the land to test Israel's obedience to God. The Lord wanted to see if the people would keep the commandments He had given their ancestors through Moses. Having pagan neighbors close by would show whether Israel truly loved God or would copy their idols.

Instead of driving out the pagan nations, the Israelites settled down and lived right among them. They shared the land with Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites as if they were friendly neighbors. By settling down with them, Israel compromised and treated God's holy land as shared ground.

The Israelites broke God's direct command by intermarrying with the pagan peoples around them. They gave their daughters to Canaanite sons and took Canaanite daughters for their own sons. These family ties pulled the Israelites away from God and led them directly into serving false gods.

The Israelites did what was evil in God's eyes and completely forgot the Lord, who had protected them. Instead, they began worshiping Baal, the male pagan god of nature, and the Asherahs, goddess poles set up in sacred tree groves. Forgetting God always opens the door to false worship.

God's anger burned against Israel for abandoning Him, so He handed them over to a foreign ruler. Cushan-rishathaim, a king from Mesopotamia far to the northeast, conquered them. The Israelites were forced to serve him and pay heavy taxes for eight years.

After eight years of harsh treatment, the Israelites finally cried out to the Lord for help. God showed them mercy and raised up Othniel to rescue them. Othniel was Caleb's younger brother and had already proven himself as a brave warrior in earlier battles.

The Holy Spirit came upon Othniel, giving him special wisdom, courage, and authority to lead. He first served as Israel's judge by correcting the people and leading them back to God, and then he went out to fight. With God's power backing him, Othniel completely defeated the king of Mesopotamia.

Because of Othniel's faithful leadership, the land enjoyed forty years of peaceful rest. God kept Israel safe and free throughout Othniel's life. When Othniel died, his passing marked the end of a long, blessed season of calm.

Once Othniel was gone, the Israelites drifted back into evil and worshiped idols again. Because of their sin, the Lord gave Eglon, the king of Moab, the strength to overpower Israel. God used this foreign king as a tool of discipline to wake up His unfaithful people.

Eglon formed an alliance with the Ammonites and Amalekites, two long-time enemies of Israel. Together they invaded the land, defeated the Israelites, and seized Jericho, the City of Palms. Setting up a stronghold there allowed the Moabites to control the river crossing and rule over Israel.

The Israelites remained under King Eglon's harsh rule for eighteen years. This period of slavery lasted more than twice as long as their previous one under Mesopotamia. When people repeatedly turn back to sin, their troubles often grow longer and heavier.

In their misery, the Israelites turned back and cried out to the Lord again. God answered by raising up Ehud, a left-handed man from the tribe of Benjamin, to save them. The Israelites chose Ehud to lead the group carrying their yearly tribute payment to King Eglon.

Ehud secretly made a double-edged dagger about eighteen inches long for his mission. Because he was left-handed, he strapped the weapon under his robe onto his right thigh. Palace guards typically checked the left thigh for weapons, so Ehud's dagger went unnoticed.

Ehud arrived at the palace and presented the tribute payment to King Eglon. The text notes that Eglon was an unusually fat man. This detail explains why the king could not move quickly and how the dagger was later hidden by his body.

After presenting the tribute, Ehud escorted the men who had helped carry the gifts part of the way home. Sending them away kept them safe from any danger when he carried out his plan. It also made the king believe that the official business was completely finished.

When Ehud reached the stone idols near Gilgal, he turned back alone to the palace. He told Eglon that he carried a confidential message just for him. The king immediately ordered silence, and all his royal attendants left the room.

Ehud approached Eglon while the king sat alone in his cool, private rooftop chamber. Ehud told him that he had a message from God for him, and the king stood up from his seat out of respect. Standing up left the heavy king completely open and unguarded.

Ehud reached with his left hand, drew the dagger from his right thigh, and drove it deep into Eglon's belly. The blow was struck with such force that the entire handle disappeared inside the wound, and the king's thick fat closed over the blade. Eglon collapsed and died immediately as his bowels emptied out.

After killing the king, Ehud stepped out onto the porch or front hallway. He shut the doors of the private upper room and locked them securely behind him. Locking the doors gave him the precious time he needed to escape without raising alarm.

After Ehud left, Eglon's servants came back and found the doors of the upper room locked. They assumed the king was using the toilet in the cool room. Out of respect for their master's privacy, they waited outside and did not disturb him.

The servants waited so long that they began to feel embarrassed and deeply concerned. Finally, they took a key and unlocked the doors to investigate. When they walked in, they discovered their master lying dead on the floor.

While the servants delayed outside the locked doors, Ehud had plenty of time to get away. He slipped past the stone idols near Gilgal and reached the wooded area of Seirah. Their long delay saved his life and allowed him to organize the next move.

When Ehud reached Seirah, he blew a ram's horn throughout the hill country of Ephraim to sound the call to battle. The Israelites heard the alarm, came down from the hills, and gathered under his leadership. With their oppressor dead, the people were ready to fight for their freedom.

Ehud urged the men to follow him, declaring that the Lord had already handed the Moabites over to them. The Israelites marched down and took control of the shallow crossing places of the Jordan River leading back to Moab. By holding these river fords, they trapped the enemy forces and prevented anyone from escaping.

During the fighting, the Israelites struck down about ten thousand Moabite soldiers. These were strong, experienced, and brave warriors who had enforced Moab's rule over Israel. Yet despite their strength, not a single one managed to escape across the river.

That day Moab was completely brought under Israel's control, ending eighteen years of harsh domination. Following this victory, the land enjoyed eighty years of peace, the longest period of rest recorded in the book of Judges. God showed that when His people turn back to Him, He can grant them long-lasting freedom.

After Ehud, Shamgar son of Anath arose to deliver Israel from Philistine raiders in the southwest. Using only an oxgoad—an eight-foot farming pole with an iron spike—Shamgar struck down six hundred Philistines. God proved that He can use humble people and ordinary tools to win great victories for His people.
